clue.text: Pretty Polly's London home

parts.note: the music-hall song 'Pretty Polly Perkins' places its heroine in a district of west London, giving the full name of her home

explanation.surface: A question about where a pretty girl named Polly lives in London.
explanation.walkthrough: The Victorian song 'Pretty Polly Perkins of Paddington Green' supplies the answer; Paddington is a district of west London.
explanation.definitionFit: The popular song names this London district as the place where its heroine Polly Perkins lives.

clue.text: No subject for a glee-party

parts.note: a glee is a cheerful part-song sung by a glee club, so a mournful funeral song would be out of place there

explanation.surface: A remark about what a group of glee-singers would never choose.
explanation.walkthrough: A glee is an unaccompanied part-song for several voices, not just merriment; a mournful lament for the dead suits neither sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A lament sung at a funeral is gloomy, the opposite of the cheerful songs of a glee club.

clue.text: 8 across is Negro

indicators.note: the solution at 8 across means to throw into disorder, so it tells the solver to rearrange the letters that follow

explanation.surface: A statement that the entry at 8 across is a racial description.
explanation.walkthrough: The indicator is borrowed from another light: 8 across is DERANGE, so 'is Negro' is to be deranged. The old-style clue gives no separate definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue is pure wordplay; the rearranged letters form the verb meaning pays no attention to or disregards.

clue.text: Follow it, wrote Tennyson

parts.note: Tennyson's poem 'Merlin and the ...' ends with the command to follow a glimmer of light

explanation.surface: A literary note that Tennyson urged readers to follow something.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's late poem 'Merlin and the Gleam' ends 'Follow the Gleam', a glimmer standing for the poet's ideal.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's closing line urges the reader to follow a faint flash of light, the poet's guiding vision.

clue.text: Tenders round finish

indicators.note: the bids are wrapped around the word for a conclusion, enclosing it

parts.note: tenders are offers, as in bids for a contract
a finish is an end

explanation.surface: Bids for a contract go round until the finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tenders' looks like a verb or the noun for small boats, but means bids. Like many clues of its era, this one gives no separate definition: the wordplay alone builds the word for culprits.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue is pure wordplay; the letters build the word for lawbreakers or culprits.

clue.text: Not a happy lead, on the face of it

definitions.text: Not a happy lead, on the face of it

parts.note: grim means stern and unhappy
an ace is a lead card, played to lead a trick at cards

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a lead role or opening card looks unpromising at first sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the face of it' seems to mean 'apparently' but is literal: the unhappy expression is worn on the face. An ace is a common opening lead at bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: A twisted look of displeasure is an unhappy expression shown on the face.

clue.text: Unrehearsed

parts.note: done on the spot without preparation, as a speech given off the cuff

explanation.definitionFit: The Latin-derived word describes a speech or performance given spontaneously, without any preparation.

clue.text: Upset a grandee

indicators.note: to upset something is to knock it over and disorder it, so the letters of the nobleman are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone offends a Spanish nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' rearranges GRANDEE, and the whole clue also says what the answer does: to unsettle a nobleman's mind.
explanation.definitionFit: To unbalance someone mentally or throw them into disorder is to upset them badly.

clue.text: It's sad to play the gramophone long after bedtime

parts.note: playing a record means putting a disc on the turntable, so it is 'disc on'
very late at night is 'so late'

explanation.surface: A complaint about a neighbour playing records far into the night.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as DISC ON SO LATE: a record put on so late at night.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone utterly unhappy and beyond comfort is sad in the deepest way.

clue.text: Frying fruit is one way to waste time

definitions.meaning: a piece of fruit dipped in batter and fried

explanation.surface: Standing over a pan frying fruit is a pleasant way to idle away the hours.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun is a battered fried snack; the verb, usually with 'away', means to squander time or money.

clue.text: When will the latest Russian note arrive?

definitions.text: When will the latest Russian note arrive?

parts.words: When will the latest Russian note arrive
parts.note: a note from Soviet Russia would be a letter from the Reds, arriving on a day named for it; really the phrase means a special occasion

explanation.surface: A question about the date of the next diplomatic note from Moscow.
explanation.walkthrough: In the 1930s 'Red' meant Soviet, so a Russian note is a Red letter. The phrase really means a memorable day, from saints' days printed in red in calendars.
explanation.definitionFit: Church calendars marked feast days in red ink, so the phrase came to mean any special, memorable occasion.

clue.text: He's not a grown-up cowboy

parts.note: a steer is a young bullock, so a man in charge of steers could jokingly be a herder of not-yet-grown cattle; really he is the person at the helm

explanation.surface: A remark that some man is merely a boyish cowboy.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as 'steers man': a cowboy minds steers (young castrated cattle). The real meaning is the helmsman of a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: The pun treats the helmsman as a herder of young bullocks, a cowman whose cattle are not full-grown.

clue.text: No quadruped is so ready to do battle

definitions.text: No quadruped is so ready to do battle

parts.words: No quadruped is so ready to do battle
parts.note: four-legged beasts have legs, not arms, so none of them is in that state; the state also means equipped with weapons for a fight

explanation.surface: A claim that no four-footed animal is more eager for a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'so' points to a state no quadruped can be in: having arms. The second sense, carrying weapons, means ready for battle.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone carrying weapons is equipped and prepared to fight; quadrupeds lack upper limbs, so none has that limb-based quality.

clue.text: Behaved disagreeably ?

parts.note: read as 'acted in a dis-agreeing way', that is, took the other side rather than behaving rudely

explanation.surface: Someone acted unpleasantly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disagreeably' looks like 'rudely' but is meant literally: by disagreeing, as one who stood against a proposal.
explanation.definitionFit: Setting oneself against a view is the literal way of acting in disagreement with it.

clue.text: The detective blushes more when not turning up

parts.note: one who blushes more is rosier, more pink in the face

indicators.note: in a down clue, a word turning up is read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A detective goes redder when someone fails to appear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning up' reverses NOT to TON; it looks like 'not arriving'. Allan Pinkerton founded the famous American detective agency.
explanation.definitionFit: Allan Pinkerton was a celebrated American private investigator whose agency gave its name to detectives generally.

clue.text: Ted's a peer, but violent

indicators.note: a violent upheaval throws things into disorder, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Ted is a nobleman, yet he is given to violence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'violent' rearranges TED'S A PEER and also describes the answer, used in its old sense of reckless and lawless.
explanation.definitionFit: A desperate man is reckless and ready for violence, like a desperado willing to do anything.

clue.text: Painful to behold

parts.note: something so ugly that looking at it seems to hurt the viewer's sight

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a noun for an ugly sight; read literally, the compound says the eye is made sore by looking.
explanation.definitionFit: An ugly building or object is said to hurt the eyes, being unpleasant to look at.

clue.text: "How many po' —— 'll be kotched' out late?" (Harris)

definitions.text: "How many po' —— 'll be kotched' out late?" (Harris)

parts.words: "How many po' —— 'll be kotched' out late?" (Harris)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Joel Chandler Harris's Uncle Remus stories, in dialect: how many poor wrongdoers will be caught out late

explanation.surface: A line of dialect quotation with a gap to complete.
explanation.walkthrough: Joel Chandler Harris wrote the Uncle Remus tales in Southern dialect: 'po'' is poor and 'kotched' is caught. The missing word is the people who will be caught out on Judgement Day.
explanation.definitionFit: The quoted line fears for poor wrongdoers caught unprepared, and the gap needs the plural word for wrongdoers against God.

clue.text: The heart of the matter, — to the French driver

definitions.meaning: the core or most important quality of something
in French the word means petrol, so it is what a French motorist calls fuel

explanation.surface: The core issue, which a French motorist also knows by name.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash in the clue stands for the same word: a French driver fills up with it, since it is French for petrol.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the core of something in English and is the ordinary French word for petrol.

clue.text: Wise man

parts.note: the Latin name of our species, Homo sapiens, means wise man, so the word is both 'wise' and a word for a human

explanation.walkthrough: The clue translates the Latin of Homo sapiens; the answer, from the same root, means wise.
explanation.definitionFit: The word comes from Latin sapiens, meaning knowing or judicious, the root of the scientific name for humankind.

clue.text: You may find it in a chapel, I can't!

definitions.text: You may find it in a chapel, I can't!

indicators.note: the bird is to be looked for inside the run of letters that follows, concealed there

explanation.surface: Someone insists that a thing can be found in a chapel, while admitting they cannot find it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'find it in' points inside CHAPEL, I CAN'T. Fittingly, the bird is a church emblem: the pelican feeding its young on its own blood symbolises Christ.
explanation.definitionFit: The large-billed water bird is carved in churches as a symbol of Christ's sacrifice.

clue.text: The first city in the land?

definitions.text: The first city in the land?

parts.words: The first city in the land
parts.note: a city that comes first could be said to lead the others, and one Yorkshire city's name sounds like that verb

explanation.surface: A question about which city ranks highest in the country.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a pun: the Yorkshire city Leeds is pronounced like 'leads', so it is the city that comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: The Yorkshire city's name puns on the verb for coming first or being in front.

clue.text: Whereupon one need take no steps to get up in the world

definitions.text: Whereupon one need take no steps to get up in the world

parts.words: Whereupon one need take no steps to get up in the world
parts.note: on a moving staircase a rider rises without climbing; 'get up in the world' usually means prosper

explanation.surface: Advice that one can rise in society without effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get up in the world' suggests social advancement and 'take no steps' suggests no effort; literally, the moving stairs carry you upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A moving staircase lifts a standing passenger to the next floor with no climbing required.

clue.text: Edict which is quoted all wrong here

indicators.note: letters set out all wrong are in the wrong order and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: A decree that has been quoted inaccurately in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all wrong' rearranges EDICT; 'here' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: A passage that has been referred to or mentioned as an authority has been quoted.

clue.text: This is the way to hunt

definitions.text: This is the way to hunt

parts.words: This is the way to hunt
parts.note: a hunter follows the track or scent left by the quarry, and the word also means to pursue it

explanation.walkthrough: 'way' is both method and path: the answer is the track left by the quarry, and also the verb for following it.
explanation.definitionFit: A path or scent left by an animal is what hunters follow, and following it is tracking it.

clue.text: Summer time was no concern of her bank

definitions.text: Summer time was no concern of her bank

parts.words: Summer time was no concern of her bank
parts.note: in A Midsummer Night's Dream the fairy queen sleeps on 'a bank where the wild thyme blows', so it is the herb, not the clock time, that grows there

explanation.surface: A banker paying no attention to the change to summer time.
explanation.walkthrough: Oberon's speech in A Midsummer Night's Dream describes the fairy queen's bank where wild thyme grows; 'time' is a pun on thyme, and 'bank' is a slope, not a money business.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's fairy queen sleeps on a flowery slope covered in thyme, the herb whose name sounds like time.

clue.text: Wrap your coat round Tom and let's have some music.!

indicators.note: the reworked coat goes around the male animal, enclosing it
to wrap a coat about oneself twists it into a new shape, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: Someone bundles up a man called Tom in a coat and then suggests some music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tom' looks like a man's name but is a male cat. 'Wrap' scrambles the coat into TOCA, which 'round' then places around the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A toccata is a keyboard piece showing off fast fingerwork, so it is a piece of music.

clue.text: How Herbert went to. Westminster ?

parts.note: the humorist A. P. Herbert entered Parliament in 1935 as a member for Oxford University with no party label

explanation.surface: A question about how a man called Herbert travelled to Westminster.
explanation.walkthrough: Westminster stands for the House of Commons. A. P. Herbert, the writer, sat there as a non-party member, so he went there without a party.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbert was elected without party backing, so he went into Parliament on his own account, beholden to nobody.
